senses.definition: A commissioned officer in an armed military organization, typically the highest rank before flag officer ranks (generals). It is generally found in armies, air forces or naval infantry (marines).

quotes.text: The colonel and his sponsor made a queer contrast: Greystone long and stringy, with a face that seemed as if a cold wind was eternally playing on it. […] But there was not a more lascivious reprobate and gourmand in all London than this same Greystone.
quotes.reference: 1908, W[illiam] B[lair] M[orton] Ferguson, chapter I, in Zollenstein, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:

senses.definition: (historical) A military leader, distinct from the modern professional military rank.

quotes.text: General Charles-Maximilian Fiennes was made colonel of the army.
quotes.reference: 2009, Ranulph Fiennes, chapter 21, in Mad Dogs and Englishmen: An Expedition Round My Family, London: Hodder & Stoughton, →ISBN, page 284:

senses.definition: An honorary civilian title bestowed by some southern US states, most commonly Kentucky; notably Colonel Sanders of KFC.

quotes.text: "Colonel" was often used as an honorific, indicating no actual military service: between 1792 and 1916, according to Ron Bryant, a curator at the Kentucky Historical Society, 400 of the 650 colonels commissioned were honorary.
quotes.reference: 2002, Kate Chopin and Anna Julia Cooper, “Critiquing Kentucky and the South”, in The Southern Literary Journal, volume 35, number 1, page 127:

senses.definition: (Southern US, dated) An informal title used to address an elderly man.
(US) A form of address for an auctioneer, from the American Civil War practice of commanding officers organizing the public sale of seized goods.
(intransitive) To act as or like a colonel.

quotes.text:
Then did Sir Knight abandon dwelling,
 And out he rode Colonelling.
